etymology: From the Old English cearu, “care, sorrow, anxiety,” with the suffix -ful; hence full of care. The modern sense “cautious” is a softening; in the KJV the word means anxious, fretful, laden with worry.
biblical_def: To be careful in the Authorized Version is not to be cautious but to be full of care — anxious, fretting, distracted with worry. The modern reader hears the word as a counsel of prudence and reads the very opposite of the apostle’s meaning, for Paul commands the thing our ears think he commends: “Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God” (Php 4:6). He does not forbid foresight; he forbids the gnawing anxiety that has no God to carry it. So the LORD Himself rebuked the busy sister: “Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things” (Luk 10:41) — cumbered with much serving while the one thing needful sat untouched at His feet. To be careful is to be Martha; to be free of care is to be Mary. The word can also name the anxiety a man is delivered from. The tree planted by the waters “shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit” (Jer 17:8), because its roots are in the river and not in the weather. There is the whole doctrine: the believer is not careful, because his root is elsewhere. The remedy is not stoic calm but a Person to whom the care is handed: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” (1Pe 5:7). Our care is real; He simply bids us give it to One who cares more.
webster_summary: Full of care; anxious; solicitous; troubled about the event — not the modern “cautious.”
webster_full: CAREFUL, full of care; anxious; solicitous; troubled about the event.
From Old English cearu, “care, sorrow,” with -ful; laden with care.
The modern “cautious” softens a word that once meant fretful anxiety.
Paul forbids it: “Be careful for nothing” (Php 4:6).
Martha was careful and troubled about many things (Luk 10:41).
scriptures: Php 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things:
Jer 17:8

For he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth out her roots by the river, and shall not see when heat cometh, but her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought, neither shall cease from yielding fruit.
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
corruption_summary: An honest drift from “full of care” to “cautious”; the word recovers Christ’s command against anxiety and His bidding to cast our care on Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The drift here is gentle, but it inverts a command. The modern ear hears “be careful” as sober counsel and reads Php 4:6 as though Paul forbade recklessness; but the apostle forbids the opposite — the anxious, fretting care that has no God to carry it. To be careful in the AV is to be Martha, cumbered and troubled about many things while the one thing needful goes untended. A reader who misses the word will hear a call to prudence where the Spirit means a rebuke to worry, and will comfort his anxiety with the very verse that condemns it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the cure Scripture gives for care, which is not stoic indifference but a Person. The believer is not careful, not because he has schooled himself to feel nothing, but because his root is in the river and not in the weather (Jer 17:8), and because he has One to whom the whole weight may be handed: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” (1Pe 5:7). Care is not abolished; it is transferred. The anxious heart is bidden to unload — by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving — upon a Father whose care for us is greater than our care for ourselves.

etymology: From care + -less, “without care”; hence free from anxiety, secure, at ease. The modern sense “negligent” is a later hardening; in the KJV it means unsuspecting, dwelling in a false peace.
biblical_def: Careless in the KJV is the exact reverse of its modern sense. It does not mean negligent or slovenly; it means free from care — secure, at ease, unsuspecting, dwelling without a guard because no danger is felt. It is almost always a word of judgment waiting to fall. The men of Laish “dwelt careless, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure” (Jdg 18:7), with no magistrate and no wall, and the tribe of Dan fell upon them and burned their city. Their carelessness was not laziness but a false peace, and it was ripe fruit ready for the reaper. So Isaiah cries to the women of Jerusalem, “Rise up, ye women that are at ease; hear my voice, ye careless daughters” (Isa 32:9), and again, “Tremble, ye women that are at ease; be troubled, ye careless ones” (Isa 32:11) — the careless ease of a city that would not believe the harvest could fail or the enemy could come. The word reaches its height in the taunt over Nineveh, “the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me” (Zep 2:15) — a blasphemy only a careless heart could speak, and a desolation only the LORD could send. To be careless in this sense is the sin of the secure: the soul so settled in its ease that it has forgotten God, forgotten judgment, and mistaken a lull for a covenant.
webster_summary: Free from care; secure; unconcerned; heedless of danger — not the modern “negligent.”
webster_full: CARELESS, free from care or anxiety; secure; unconcerned; heedless of danger.
From care + -less, “without care”; the opposite of anxious.
The modern “negligent” hardens a word that meant a false security.
Laish dwelt careless, quiet and secure, and fell (Jdg 18:7).
The careless daughters of Zion were bidden to tremble (Isa 32:11).

Then the five men departed, and came to Laish, and saw the people that were therein, how they dwelt careless, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure; and there was no magistrate in the land, that might put them to shame in any thing; and they were far from the Zidonians, and had no business with any man.
Isa 32:9
Rise up, ye women that are at ease; hear my voice, ye careless daughters; give ear unto my speech.
Tremble, ye women that are at ease; be troubled, ye careless ones: strip you, and make you bare, and gird sackcloth upon your loins.
Zep 2:15

This is the rejoicing city that dwelt carelessly, that said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me: how is she become a desolation, a place for beasts to lie down in! every one that passeth by her shall hiss, and wag his hand.
corruption_summary: An honest drift from “free of care” to “negligent”; the word recovers the sin of the secure — the false peace that has forgotten God and judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears “careless” and thinks of sloppiness, a job done without pains; the AV means something graver — a soul so free of care, so settled and secure, that it has ceased to watch. The careless daughters of Isaiah were not slovenly but at ease; the men of Laish were not lazy but unsuspecting; Nineveh dwelt carelessly and said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me. A reader who reads only negligence will miss that carelessness in the KJV is a spiritual condition — the complacent security of a heart that has mistaken a lull for a covenant.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is watchfulness. Scripture treats false security as ripe fruit for judgment: the city that dwells carelessly, saying peace and safety, is the city upon which sudden destruction comes. The Christian is bidden to the opposite temper — to watch, to be sober, to take heed lest he fall, to keep his ward when no eye sees. This is not anxiety, for the careful heart and the careless heart are both rebuked; it is vigilance. The saint neither frets like the careful nor dozes like the careless, but watches, because he knows the night is far spent and his Lord may come at an hour he thinks not.
roots_summary: The word means free from care — secure, at ease, unsuspecting, not merely negligent.
roots_lines: Careless — care + -less, “without care.”
It means secure, at ease, dwelling in a false peace.

etymology: From the Latin instans, present participle of instare, “to stand upon, to press upon, to urge” (in, “upon,” + stare, “to stand”); hence urgent, pressing. The modern noun for a moment came from the sense of a pressing, present point of time.
biblical_def: Instant in the KJV is never the modern noun for a fleeting moment; it is an adjective and adverb meaning urgent, pressing, insistent — to be instant is to press a matter hard and not let go. Paul bids the Romans be “continuing instant in prayer” (Rom 12:12), not praying briefly but praying with an unrelenting importunity that keeps its hold on God. He charges Timothy, “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) — stand to it, urge it, press it whether the hour seems fit or not, with all longsuffering and doctrine. The word describes the earnestness of men in dead earnest. The elders of the Jews “besought him instantly” for the centurion (Luk 7:4), pressing the Lord with reasons; and in a darker use the same insistence turns murderous, for the crowd before Pilate “were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified” (Luk 23:23), and their instancy prevailed. So the word cuts both ways: the same pressing urgency that storms heaven in prayer can storm a judgment-hall for blood. What Scripture commends is holy instancy — the widow who wearied the unjust judge, the friend at midnight who would not be denied, the wrestling Jacob who said, I will not let thee go except thou bless me. The Christian’s prayer is not a polite request lightly withdrawn; it is an instant, importunate, God-honouring refusal to release the promise.
webster_summary: Urgent; pressing; earnest and importunate — not a fleeting moment.
webster_full: INSTANT, urgent; pressing; earnest; importunate.
From Latin instare, “to stand upon, to press upon.”
The modern noun for a moment came of a pressing point of time.
Continuing instant in prayer (Rom 12:12); instant in season (2Ti 4:2).
The crowd was instant with loud voices for the crucifixion (Luk 23:23).
scriptures: Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer;

And when they came to Jesus, they besought him instantly, saying, That he was worthy for whom he should do this:
And they were instant with loud voices, requiring that he might be crucified. And the voices of them and of the chief priests prevailed.
corruption_summary: An honest drift from “urgent” to “a moment”; the word recovers the importunate, pressing earnestness Scripture commends in prayer and preaching.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reader knows “instant” only as a name for the briefest span of time, or as a promise of coffee made without waiting; and so he cannot hear what Paul means by “continuing instant in prayer.” The AV’s instant is not a moment but an urgency — a pressing, insistent, importunate holding-on. To read the modern sense into Rom 12:12 is to make the verse counsel brief prayer, when the apostle counsels unrelenting prayer — the very opposite of a passing instant.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is holy importunity. Our Lord taught it in the widow who wearied the unjust judge and the friend who knocked at midnight and would not go away; He commended the woman of Canaan whose faith would not be refused. To be instant is to press the promise and not let go, to preach in season and out of season, to plead until the blessing come. The world’s instancy can turn murderous, as the crowd was instant for the crucifixion; but sanctified, it is the wrestling of Jacob, who said, I will not let thee go except thou bless me. God is not wearied by such prayer; He is honoured by it.
roots_summary: The word means urgent, pressing, importunate — not a fleeting moment.
roots_lines: Instant — Latin instare, “to press upon, to urge.”
It means urgent, insistent, earnest in the pursuit.
The modern noun for a moment is a later branch of the word.

To be instant is to press the matter hard, in season and out of season.
The crowd was instant for the crucifixion: even instancy can turn murderous.

etymology: From the Latin studium, “zeal, eagerness, painstaking application,” from studēre, “to be diligent, to give oneself earnestly”; hence to endeavour, to be earnest. The narrowing to “read books” is a late specialising of a much broader word.
biblical_def: To study in the KJV rarely means to read a book; it means to be diligent, to give oneself earnestly to a thing, to make it one’s serious business and endeavour. When Paul writes, “Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15), he is not commanding an hour with the scrolls but a whole labour of the soul — be diligent, give thy diligence, spend thyself to stand approved before God. So he bids the Thessalonians “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — where the modern ear hears a contradiction, for how does one study to be quiet? The AV means: make it your ambition, your earnest aim, to lead a quiet and industrious life. The heart is the seat of this study. “The heart of the righteous studieth to answer” (Pro 15:28) — it weighs, ponders, and prepares a careful word, while the mouth of the wicked pours out evil unweighed. The word does carry its bookish sense once, and there with a warning: “of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh” (Ecc 12:12). But the great biblical study is not the wearying of the flesh over many books; it is the diligent bending of the whole man toward the will of God. To study is to be earnest, and the thing God approves is not the reader merely but the workman.
webster_summary: To apply the mind earnestly; to be diligent; to endeavour — not merely to read.
webster_full: STUDY, to apply the mind earnestly; to be diligent; to endeavour.
From Latin studium, “zeal, eager application.”
The narrowing to “read books” is a late specialising of the word.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God (2Ti 2:15).
Study to be quiet, and to do your own business (1Th 4:11).
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
The heart of the righteous studieth to answer: but the mouth of the wicked poureth out evil things.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
corruption_summary: An honest drift from “be diligent” to “read books”; the word recovers earnest, whole-souled diligence in the service and knowledge of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear hears “study” and pictures a desk, a lamp, and a book; and so “study to be quiet” sounds like nonsense — how does one read one’s way to quietness? The AV means diligence, earnest endeavour, the whole bent of the man toward a thing. To narrow it to bookwork is to lose the force of 2Ti 2:15, which is not a call to more reading but to labour to stand approved before God as an unashamed workman.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is diligence as a duty of the whole life, not merely of the desk. Scripture bids us study to be quiet, to do our own business, to work with our hands; the heart of the righteous studieth to answer, weighing a careful word before it speaks. There is a warning, too, against study cut loose from its end: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh. The great study God approves is not the wearying of the flesh over many volumes but the earnest bending of the soul toward His will — to know it, and to do it, and to stand at last a workman that needeth not to be ashamed.
roots_summary: The word means to be diligent, to give oneself earnestly — not merely to read.
roots_lines: Study — Latin studium, “zeal, eager application.”
It means to endeavour, to be diligent, to make one’s business.

etymology: From the Middle English stakeren, from the Old Norse stakra, “to push, to totter”; hence to reel, to sway, to lose one’s footing, and figuratively to waver in mind or faith.
biblical_def: To stagger in the KJV is to waver, to reel, to be irresolute — the unsteadiness of a man who cannot hold his footing, whether in body or in faith. Its noblest use is a negative: of Abraham it is written that “he staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God” (Rom 4:20). There is the picture — a promise so staggering that a man of a hundred years and a dead womb might well have reeled under it, and Abraham stood. To stagger is what unbelief does when the promise seems too great; faith plants its feet and does not lurch. The word’s other uses are of drunken instability. The mariners in the storm “reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits’ end” (Psa 107:27), helpless until they cry unto the LORD. Isaiah sees a people drunk without wine: “they are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink” (Isa 29:9) — a spiritual stupor sent as judgment, a reeling of the soul that no cup poured. And in the day of the LORD “the earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard” (Isa 24:20), staggering under the weight of its transgression until it falls and rises no more. So the word sets two men side by side: the world staggering under judgment and its own unbelief, and the believer who, leaning on a naked promise, staggers not.
webster_summary: To reel; to totter; to waver in mind or purpose.
webster_full: STAGGER, to reel; to totter; to move unsteadily; to waver or hesitate.
From Old Norse stakra, “to push, to totter.”
Figuratively, to waver in mind or in faith before a promise.
Abraham staggered not at the promise of God (Rom 4:20).
The drunken reel and stagger at their wits’ end (Psa 107:27).
scriptures: Rom 4:20
He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God;
They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man, and are at their wits' end.
Isa 29:9
Stay yourselves, and wonder; cry ye out, and cry: they are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink.
The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again.
corruption_summary: The word is little changed, but it recovers a vivid picture: unbelief staggers under a great promise, while faith, like Abraham’s, plants its feet and does not reel.
corruption_paragraphs: Here the modern sense and the old sense nearly agree — to stagger is still to reel — and the drift is only that we have half-forgotten its figurative reach. The KJV uses it for the soul as much as the body: a man staggers at the promise of God when unbelief makes the promise seem too great to stand under. The peril is not that the modern reader misreads the word but that he misses its doctrine, hearing only a drunkard’s totter where Scripture also means the wavering of a heart that will not rest on a bare word of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the steadiness of faith. Abraham staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strong in faith, giving glory to God — and that is the pattern for every believer set before a promise too large for sight. The world staggers: the wicked reel to and fro like drunken men, and the earth itself shall stagger under the weight of its transgression in the day of the LORD. But faith does not stagger, because it leans not on the likelihood of the thing promised but on the faithfulness of Him who promised. He is able also to perform; therefore the believer stands.
roots_summary: The word means to reel, to totter, to waver — in body or in faith.
roots_lines: Stagger — Old Norse stakra, “to push, to totter.”

etymology: From the Latin sincerus, “clean, pure, unmixed, whole”; hence unadulterated, without any foreign or corrupting thing. The old fancy derived it from sine cera, “without wax,” of pure honey.
biblical_def: Sincere in the KJV keeps its oldest and purest force: unmixed, unadulterated, without any foreign thing folded in. It is not first a word about honest feeling but about unmingled substance — that is sincere which has nothing added to corrupt it. So Peter bids the newborn to “desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1Pe 2:2) — pure milk, unwatered and undrugged, with no mingling of man’s doctrine to sicken the child. Paul prays that the Philippians “may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ” (Php 1:10), a heart of one metal and not an alloy. He appoints the same purity to the conscience: “in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world” (2Co 1:12) — a walk with nothing double in it, no craft folded under the profession. And he sets the feast of the church under the figure of unleavened bread: “let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1Co 5:8). Leaven is the foreign thing that spreads and sours; sincerity is the loaf with no leaven in it. Old writers loved the fancy that sincerus meant honey without wax; the sense is exact either way: the sincere heart is pure through and through, the same in the dark as in the light, one thing all the way down.
webster_summary: Pure; unmixed; unadulterated; genuine through and through.
webster_full: SINCERE, pure; unmixed; unadulterated; free from any foreign or corrupting thing.
From Latin sincerus, “clean, whole, unmingled.”
An old fancy read it sine cera, “without wax,” of pure honey.
Desire the sincere milk of the word (1Pe 2:2).
The unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1Co 5:8).
scriptures: As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
Php 1:10
That ye may approve things that are excellent; that ye may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ;

For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom, but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and more abundantly to you-ward.
Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
corruption_summary: An honest drift from “pure and unmixed” toward mere “honest feeling”; the word recovers purity of substance — the unleavened heart, the unwatered word.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern ear takes “sincere” to mean well-meant, heartfelt, honestly intended — a word about the warmth of a feeling. The AV means first a purity of substance: that is sincere which has nothing foreign mixed into it. A man may be sincere in the modern sense — earnest, heartfelt — and be sincerely wrong; but the biblical sincere milk of the word is milk with no poison stirred in, and the sincere heart is one metal and not an alloy. To reduce the word to good intentions is to lose the whole force of the unleavened loaf.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is purity through and through — the heart the same in the dark as in the light, with no leaven of malice folded under the profession. Paul prays the saints be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ, and bids them keep the feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. The mark of a sincere man is not the strength of his feeling but the singleness of his substance: no craft hidden, no double aim, no foreign thing corrupting the whole. And such purity is not native to us; it is the sincere milk of the word that grows it, and the grace of God, not fleshly wisdom, by which alone a man walks sincere in the world.
roots_summary: The word means pure, unmixed, unadulterated — genuine through and through.

etymology: From sot, a dull or stupefied person (through the Old French sot, “fool”), with the suffix -ish; hence stupid, senseless, besotted — the dullness of a mind deadened, as by drink or by idolatry.
biblical_def: Sottish is a hard word for a hard thing: stupefied, dull, senselessly foolish — the deadened wit of a man whose sin has thickened his mind until he can no longer reason. It is stronger than mere ignorance; it is a besotted stupidity, and in Scripture it is the peculiar mark of the idolater, whose false gods have made him as brainless as themselves. The LORD indicts His people through Jeremiah: “my people is foolish, they have not known me; they are sottish children, and they have none understanding: they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge” (Jer 4:22). Note the terrible balance — sharp for evil, sottish for good; the sin has not dulled every faculty, only the one that turns toward God. The cause is named a few chapters on. Of the idols it is said, “they are altogether brutish and foolish: the stock is a doctrine of vanities” (Jer 10:8), and the maker sinks to the level of the thing he makes: “Every man is brutish in his knowledge: every founder is confounded by the graven image” (Jer 10:14). Men become as stupid as their gods. The psalmist marks it plainly: “A brutish man knoweth not; neither doth a fool understand this” (Psa 92:6). Here is the wages of idolatry upon the mind itself — not merely guilt but a settled dullness, a soul stupefied by the vanity it has worshipped, sottish toward the only God who could make it wise.
webster_summary: Stupid; dull; senseless; besotted in understanding.
webster_full: SOTTISH, stupid; dull; senseless; besotted; stupefied in understanding.
From sot, “a dull or stupefied person,” + -ish.
It names a deadened mind, as of drink — here, of idolatry.
My people are sottish children, with none understanding (Jer 4:22).
The idol-maker is brutish in his knowledge (Jer 10:14).

For my people is foolish, they have not known me; they are sottish children, and they have none understanding: they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.
Jer 10:8
But they are altogether brutish and foolish: the stock is a doctrine of vanities.

corruption_summary: A word little used and half-lost; it recovers the deadening of the mind that idolatry works — men made as stupid as the gods they serve.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has all but fallen out of use, and where it survives it means merely tipsy or foolish; the reader who meets “sottish children” in Jeremiah may take it for a mild scolding. It is not mild. Sottish names a stupefied, deadened understanding — a mind so thickened by sin that it can no longer reason toward God, though it stays sharp enough to devise evil. It is the special dullness of the idolater, and Scripture names the cause plainly: the man sinks to the level of the thing he worships.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that idolatry stupefies the soul. The LORD’s complaint through Jeremiah is not only that His people are guilty but that they are dull: sottish children with none understanding, wise to do evil but ignorant of good. Their gods are a doctrine of vanities, and every man that makes them is brutish in his knowledge. This is judgment as well as sin — a settled deadness sent upon the mind that prefers a lie. The remedy is the same LORD who diagnoses the disease: only He can give a heart to know Him, taking away the stony, sottish heart and giving a heart of flesh that understands.
roots_summary: The word means stupefied, dull, senseless — the deadened mind of the idolater.
roots_lines: Sottish — from sot, “a stupefied person,” + -ish.
It means stupid, senseless, besotted in understanding.
It names a mind deadened, as by drink or by idolatry.
Sottish children, with none understanding (Jer 4:22).
The idol-maker is brutish in his knowledge (Jer 10:14).
usage: Sottish children with none understanding: idolatry deadens the mind that serves it.
Wise to do evil, sottish toward good — the dullness falls on the faculty that turns to God.
The maker of idols grows as brutish as the thing he makes.

etymology: From the Middle English seely, Old English sælig, “happy, blessed, innocent,” which drifted through “harmless” and “helpless” to “simple.” In the KJV it means simple, defenceless, easily led — not the modern “absurd.”
biblical_def: Silly in the KJV does not mean goofy or absurd; it means simple, gullible, defenceless — easily led, easily deceived, easily preyed upon. It is the older sense of the word, near to seely, “harmless, helpless,” and it names not a comic figure but a vulnerable one. Paul warns of false teachers who “creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts” (2Ti 3:6) — not stupid women but unstable, undiscerning ones, an easy capture for every smooth deceiver because they have no anchor in the truth. Job uses it of the man undone by his own passions: “wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one” (Job 5:2), the simple soul destroyed by the sins it never guarded against. Hosea makes it a bird: “Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart” (Hos 7:11) — fluttering to Egypt, then to Assyria, trusting every foreign nest and possessing none of the wit to see the fowler. And Solomon gives the very definition: “The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going” (Pro 14:15). There is the silly soul — it believes every word, follows every teacher, is tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine. The remedy is not native cleverness but a mind established in Scripture, that it be no more a child, but able to try the spirits whether they be of God.
webster_summary: Simple; harmless; easily led or deceived — not the modern “absurd.”
webster_full: SILLY, simple; harmless; helpless; easily led or deceived.
From Middle English seely, “happy, innocent, harmless.”
It drifted through “helpless” to “simple”; not the modern “absurd.”
False teachers lead captive silly women (2Ti 3:6).
Ephraim is like a silly dove without heart (Hos 7:11).
scriptures: For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts,
Job 5:2
For wrath killeth the foolish man, and envy slayeth the silly one.
Hos 7:11
Ephraim also is like a silly dove without heart: they call to Egypt, they go to Assyria.
The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
corruption_summary: An honest drift from “simple and helpless” to “absurd”; the word recovers the danger of the undiscerning soul, easy prey for every deceiver.
corruption_paragraphs: To the modern ear “silly” is comic — foolish in a harmless, laughable way — and so “silly women” in 2Ti 3:6 sounds like a slur on their intelligence. It is nothing so light. The AV’s silly is the simple, the gullible, the defenceless: not stupid but undiscerning, an easy capture for the false teacher because the soul has no anchor in the truth. The word names a peril, not a joke — the vulnerability of the unestablished heart that believes every word.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is discernment. Solomon draws the line exactly: the simple believeth every word, but the prudent man looketh well to his going. The silly dove flies to Egypt and then to Assyria, trusting every nest; the silly women are led captive by men who creep into houses. The cure is not native cleverness but a mind established in Scripture, no more a child tossed to and fro with every wind of doctrine, but grown up to try the spirits whether they be of God. God does not leave His own defenceless; He gives them His word, His Spirit, and pastors to establish them, that the simple be made wise and the silly no longer led astray.
roots_summary: The word means simple, helpless, easily led — not the modern “absurd.”
roots_lines: Silly — Middle English seely, “innocent, harmless.”
It drifted through “helpless” to “simple, gullible.”
It names the undiscerning, defenceless soul, not the comic one.
False teachers lead captive silly women (2Ti 3:6).
Ephraim is like a silly dove without heart (Hos 7:11).
usage: Silly women led captive: not stupid but undiscerning, easy prey for the deceiver.
Ephraim is a silly dove, fluttering to Egypt and Assyria and never seeing the fowler.
The simple believeth every word — the silly soul is the one with no anchor in the truth.

etymology: From the Latin addicere, “to assign, to devote, to deliver over” (ad, “to,” + dicere, “to say, to adjudge”); hence to give oneself over to a thing. The modern sense of helpless bondage is a dark reversal of a word that once named willing devotion.
biblical_def: Here the drift has run clean backward, and the recovery is sweet. To us, addiction is bondage — the helpless captivity of a man mastered by a craving he hates. In the KJV to be addicted is a thing to be praised: it means to devote oneself, to give oneself over wholly, to attach one’s whole strength to a good and worthy service. Paul commends the household of Stephanas because “they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints” (1Co 16:15) — they gave themselves up to it, made it their fixed and voluntary devotion, and Paul bids the church submit to such men. The modern addict is held; the KJV addict gives — and that reversal is the whole gospel of sanctification in a word. For the truth is that every man is addicted to something; the only question is whether the master is a tyrant or the LORD. The apostles model the holy addiction: “we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4). It is commanded of every saint: “given to hospitality” (Rom 12:13), and “Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving” (Col 4:2). To be addicted to hospitality, to prayer, to the ministry of the saints — this is not bondage but the freest thing a man can do, the whole self poured out by glad choice into the service of God. Grace does not un-addict the heart; it changes the object of its devotion.
webster_summary: Devoted; given over to a pursuit — in the KJV a willing and worthy self-giving.
webster_full: ADDICTED, devoted; given over; attached by voluntary devotion to a pursuit.
From Latin addicere, “to assign, to devote, to deliver over.”
The modern sense of helpless bondage reverses a word of willing service.
The house of Stephanas addicted themselves to the ministry (1Co 16:15).
The apostles gave themselves continually to prayer (Act 6:4).
scriptures: I beseech you, brethren, (ye know the house of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints,)
Act 6:4
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
Col 4:2
Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving;
corruption_summary: A striking reversal: our “addiction” is bondage, the KJV’s is holy self-giving; the word recovers devotion to God as the freest act of the will.
corruption_paragraphs: Here the drift has run backward, and the reversal is worth naming. To us addiction means captivity — a man mastered by a craving he cannot break. In the KJV to be addicted is to devote oneself, freely and gladly, to a worthy service: the house of Stephanas addicted themselves to the ministry of the saints, and Paul holds them up for honour. The modern addict is held against his will; the KJV addict gives himself of his own. A reader who carries the modern sense into 1Co 16:15 will hear bondage where Paul means the highest liberty.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that devotion is the will’s freest act, and that every heart is addicted to something. The only question is the master. Fallen men give themselves over to their lusts and call it freedom; the saint gives himself continually to prayer and the ministry of the word, is given to hospitality, continues in prayer, and finds in that self-giving no bondage at all but the liberty for which he was made. Grace does not empty the heart of devotion; it changes the object of it — unbinding the man from the tyrant and addicting him, gladly and forever, to the LORD who bought him.
roots_summary: The word means devoted, given over — in the KJV a willing, worthy self-giving.
roots_lines: Addicted — Latin addicere, “to devote, to deliver over.”
It means to give oneself wholly to a pursuit or service.
The modern sense of bondage reverses a word of willing devotion.
Stephanas addicted himself to the ministry of the saints (1Co 16:15).
The apostles gave themselves continually to prayer (Act 6:4).
usage: Stephanas addicted himself to the ministry: our word means bondage, the KJV’s means glad devotion.
Every heart is addicted to something; grace changes the master, not the fact.
To be addicted to prayer and hospitality is the freest thing a redeemed man can do.

etymology: From un- + speakable, that which cannot be spoken; hence inexpressible, beyond the power of words. The modern drift toward “unspeakably wicked” narrows a word the KJV uses only of things too glorious to utter.
biblical_def: Unspeakable in the KJV carries no shadow of the modern “unspeakably bad”; it means simply inexpressible — too great, too full, too glorious to be uttered by any tongue. It is a word reserved for the overflow, where language breaks down before the goodness of God. Paul, having pressed the Corinthians toward liberal giving, ends not with a total but with a doxology: “Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift” (2Co 9:15) — the gift of His own Son, so vast that the apostle who has words for everything confesses he has none for this. Peter uses it of the believer’s hidden joy: loving a Christ they never saw, “in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory” (1Pe 1:8) — a gladness that runs past the edge of speech. And Paul uses it of what he heard when caught up into paradise: “he heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2Co 12:4) — here unspeakable is not merely beyond utterance but forbidden to it, a glory sealed. So the word marks the frontier of language: there is a gift, a joy, and a glory that the tongue cannot carry. Even prayer arrives there, for “the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Rom 8:26). Where the saint’s words fail, the Spirit’s unspeakable groanings take up the plea — and God, who needs no words, hears them perfectly.
webster_summary: Inexpressible; unutterable; beyond the power of speech.
webster_full: UNSPEAKABLE, inexpressible; unutterable; beyond the power of words.
From un- + speakable, that which cannot be spoken.
In the KJV it names only what is too glorious to utter.
Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift (2Co 9:15).
Joy unspeakable and full of glory (1Pe 1:8).
scriptures: Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift.
Whom having not seen, ye love; in whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory:
How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter.
Rom 8:26
Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
corruption_summary: An honest drift toward “unspeakably bad”; the word recovers its true reach — the gift, joy, and glory of God too great for any tongue.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage has darkened the word: we say “unspeakable” of horrors, of things too wicked to name; and so a reader may be jarred to find Paul giving thanks for God’s “unspeakable gift.” The AV means only inexpressible — beyond the power of words — and it reserves the word for the overflow of goodness, where language fails before the greatness of God. To hear the modern sense in it is to bring a shadow into a doxology.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the frontier of language before the glory of God. There is a gift too great to price — His own Son; a joy too full to describe — the gladness of loving a Christ unseen; a glory too holy to repeat — the words Paul heard in paradise, which it is not lawful to utter. The proper response of the soul at that frontier is not silence only but worship: thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift. And where even the saint’s words fail him in prayer, the Spirit Himself takes up the plea with groanings which cannot be uttered — so that the unspeakable God is served by an unspeakable joy, and heard through an unspeakable groaning, and praised for an unspeakable gift.
roots_summary: The word means inexpressible, unutterable — too great for any tongue.
roots_lines: Unspeakable — un- + speakable, “not to be spoken.”
It means inexpressible, beyond the power of words.
In the KJV it names only what is too glorious to utter.
Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift (2Co 9:15).
Joy unspeakable and full of glory (1Pe 1:8).
usage: “His unspeakable gift” means inexpressible, not unspeakably bad.
Joy unspeakable and full of glory: a gladness that runs past the edge of words.
Paul heard unspeakable words in paradise — a glory beyond utterance and sealed from it.
